anti_generic_signature_read: Six things stop this being generic sphere-chess. The sun and anti-sun inversion — identical star geometry rendered once in warm cream and orange and once in black and cyan at the opposite corner — is a real design idea, not decoration. Each planet is individuated by real astronomy: the Great Red Spot low on Jupiter, Saturn's actual protruding tilted ring, Uranus's band running vertically over the pole, Neptune's fine bands and dark spot, Earth's polar cap. Somebody knew that Uranus is tipped over. The rubble cells have a modelled crumbly rim around a smooth dish, so the belt has a texture you can feel. The cells around each star carry a half-sun engraving oriented so the radiation reads outward. There is micro-engraving around the cream plate's border. And the two nesting trays mean the designer thought about where the sixteen balls live when the game is over, which most game objects do not.
blind_action_read: Two people sit across the board and take turns picking a puck up by its rim — the puck is the finger-grip, the sphere is the visual head — and moving it across the grid. You steer your eight worlds over a field that is not uniform: the rubble cells are terrain, one star cluster is your home and the other is the opponent's. In the third panel a piece is standing squarely on top of the black star plate, so arriving at the opponent's star clearly is the point. Between games you drop the eight balls into the eight nests of your tray, so setting up and putting away are as much of the action as the moves are.
blind_form_read: One dominant flat slab: a rectangular grey board scored into a square grid, the base mass everything else reads against, with a plain square edge and no border art. Sixteen small vertical masses stand on it, each a low cylindrical puck about 1.7 times the diameter of the ball it carries, with a sphere seated on top through a short collar; these are the only things that stand to grabbable height. Two terrain families are set into the grid rather than standing on it: ochre rubble cells with a raised crumbly rim around a smooth circular floor, and two four-cell star clusters whose centre plates are flat, one pale cream and slightly proud with a visible lip, one pure black. About fourteen slender tapered cones are the only sharp vertical features. Two thin off-board trays lie beside the board, each with eight wells in a 2x4 grid. A very low, very horizontal object: from the side it would be almost all board.
blind_held_read: A two-player abstract strategy board game about the solar system. If I picked it up I would say I was holding a printed game board tile-set: a flat grey slab scored into a square grid, sixteen ball-on-disc playing pieces (two colour-coded armies of eight), a set of drop-in terrain tiles, and two off-board storage trays with nests. It reads as “chess, but the pieces are planets and the two home squares are a sun and an anti-sun”.
blind_relationship_read: The grid is the grammar and everything else is a word in it. One feature occupies exactly one cell: the rubble cells, the corona cells and the two star plates all sit inside single cells, and each star cluster is one plate plus three cells. The spikes are the causal signature — they rise from the star plate, two each, and from the cells around it, so the cones are the radiation the star throws off and the flat engraving on those cells is that same radiation drawn flat. The pieces relate to the cells one to one: a puck nests inside a cell footprint with clearance all round, so no piece ever touches another. Sun and anti-sun are the same geometry inverted in colour, a positive and its negative at opposite corners, which sets the whole board up as a tug between two poles. The trays sit outside the game entirely: they are the object at rest, the board is the object in play.
blind_subjects_read: Six kinds. Sixteen worlds: eight distinct spheres, each existing twice, once on a black puck and once on a white puck. Mercury, plain matte light grey, the smallest ball. Venus, cream with a single orange inlay, a stem with two arms splaying downward. Earth, mid-blue with bright green continents and a white polar cap, instantly readable. Mars, saturated red with tan patches and a small cap. Jupiter, tan with seven or eight darker bands and one deep-red oval low on the disc, unmistakably the Great Red Spot. Saturn, pale yellow with ochre bands wearing a real protruding tilted annulus that stands clear of the silhouette. Uranus, cyan with one broad white band running vertically over the pole, a flush inlay and not a ring. Neptune, deep blue with three fine bands and a storm oval. Then the sun cluster, the anti-sun cluster, twelve ochre rubble cells, about fourteen cones, and two eight-well trays.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “Eight distinct spheres, each existing twice: once on a BLACK puck and once on a WHITE puck. Two armies of eight.” And: “each a low cylindrical puck … with a sphere seated on top via a short collar”, “Every sphere is one fused body with flush colour markings.” The collar was read as part of the piece, never as a joint.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. Sixteen worlds: two armies of eight, each a globe standing on a flat 34.00 mm disc, one single printed part per piece, no assembly and no hardware.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Mercury read blind as “plain matte light grey, smallest ball” and Jupiter as the largest, and the disc was already being used as the ruler: “the puck is roughly 1.7x the diameter of the ball it carries”. The fifth-root compression was read as a deliberate gameplay decision, which is what it is.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. Rank is globe diameter, read against a constant disc, strictly increasing from Mercury to Jupiter.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: All eight planets named correctly, blind, from surface alone. “Jupiter … one deep-red oval low on the disc: unmistakably the Great Red Spot.” “Earth … bright green continent blobs and one white polar cap. Instantly readable as Earth.” “Uranus … a single broad white band running vertically over the pole … Reads correctly as Uranus tipped on its side.” Venus's mark was labelled a keyhole and, on re-inspection, is a stem with two arms splaying downward: the inverted Y.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. Each globe carries its real surface: Jupiter's Great Red Spot at 22 degrees south, Earth's continents and ice cap, Mars's albedo patches and caps, Neptune's dark spot and streaks, Uranus's single vertical band, Saturn's ring, Venus's inverted cloud Y, Mercury's albedo map.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “A rectangular grey board … scored into a square grid”; “The grid is the grammar; everything else is a word in it”; under what is flat, “The board slab itself”. The cells were read as drawn by lines and the pieces as standing on top of them.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The field is flat and the grid is cut into it as a groove. A board is read as a lattice of lines: a piece stands on the board, it does not sink into it.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Circles on land cells are never mentioned anywhere in the blind read. The whole relationship read is built on the grid as lines. The only circles seen anywhere were on the twelve belt tiles and in the two trays.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. The board must not read as a muffin tray. The Wish deleted a draft that gave all 63 cells a landing recess for exactly this reason.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “Two flat-but-textured terrain families set INTO the grid … ochre/brown rubble cells … and two four-cell star clusters”, and “Nothing else breaks the plane by more than a millimetre or two.”
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. Depth is reserved for terrain only — belt, corona wells, den — where a change of level is the rule being shown.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “Roughly 12-14 ochre/brown cells, laid in two loose clusters.” The two blocks and the dry lane between them were both visible, and a piece stands in that dry lane in the third panel. The per-cell ribs were read as “a raised, deliberately rough crumbly rim” around each tile — a tile-per-cell belt, not a slab.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The asteroid belt is twelve cocoa_brown tiles, one per cell, in two blocks with the middle file left dry, so the cut grid runs unbroken through the water.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “Three orange cells each engraved with a half-sun glyph” and “three cyan cells with the same engraved sunburst”. At 12x on the middle panel a black disc sits in a Sol corona well with orange tile visible all round its rim and no cylinder wall showing, beside a white disc showing its full wall. The drop is visible and unambiguous.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. Three sunken corona wells ring each den, in that star's own colour, their tops below the field, so a trapped world drops and reads as stripped of rank.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “Orange cells each engraved with a half-sun glyph (a semicircular arc with radiating dashes)”. At 11x the radial flames are dark incised dashes in an otherwise flat face, with no proud edge and no cast highlight.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. The corona cell's flames must be engraved, not raised: raised relief under a seated disc would make a trapped piece rock, the one thing a corona well must not do.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “About 14 slender tapered spikes, orange on the sun side and cyan on the anti-sun side”, with “more cones stand at the corners of the orange cells”, and in the relationship read they were understood as radiation thrown outward from the plate.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. Two raised tongues per corona cell, at the corners furthest from the den, so every tongue points away from the star.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Measured on an unoccluded tongue by column-profiling the cyan mask against the known disc diameter: 6.9 mm of cone body against a 7.00 mm specification, a match to 0.1 mm. The blind impression that the tongues looked tall was withdrawn; they occlude nothing.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. The corona tongues are held low enough that a corona cell can never occlude a piece anywhere on the board; nothing but the two den flames may stand up.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “A pale cream square plate that sits PROUD of the grid with a visible edge lip and micro-engraved text or dashes around its border.” The micro-engraving is the granulation. The flange edge reads as the cell line with nothing lapping over it, which the measured extents confirm.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The den plug is a 36.00 mm square flange standing proud of the field with a flat top face and granulation engraved into the corners a seated disc never covers, and it is the highest ordinary surface on the board.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Read blind as “slender tapered spikes”, “the only sharp vertical features”, “tapered flames”. No hooking, no inward curve and no horn read anywhere in the blind pass; at 12x the taper is straight and unbroken from foot to tip.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. The den flares must not read as bull horns; three reference generations failed on exactly this.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Confirmed at 12x on both copies before the Wish was revealed: “It is a flush painted/inlaid stripe, not a projecting ring — it never leaves the sphere's silhouette.” It was filed blind as an inconsistency against Saturn and then retracted on reveal as the Wish's explicit decision.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. Uranus has no rings in this set; adding them would be invention.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “Mercury — plain matte light grey, smallest ball, completely unmarked.” No craters were found because there are none; the two albedo patches were found only at 14x, very faint.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. Mercury carries a two-tone albedo map, not craters, because at this radius a crater reads as a print defect.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: “In panel three a piece is standing squarely on top of the black star plate, so arriving at the opponent's star clearly IS the point.” At 8x that piece is a white Sol disc carrying Neptune, standing on the black Anti-Sol plug — the legal winning position, read without a caption.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The win state is readable in the object: a world seats on the rival star itself, one step higher than the field.

largest_risk: That the hero does not arrive. The Wish spends its whole composition budget on one idea: a sunflower_yellow star that is “the only tall, warm, saturated mass in the frame”, with two 18 mm flames bursting off the board edge and a warm corona spread across four cells. Three individually excusable things stack against it. The reserved hero colour renders as a pale wheat less saturated than the orange tiles beside it. The flames, narrowed to 6.00 mm feet standing inside the flange by a measured overhang failure in the Wish's own 7.2 geometry, read at scene scale as two thin vertical pins rather than as flares bursting from a star. And the dark_gray field renders light, so the warm cluster has nothing dark to burn against. Blind, with no prior, the critic did not name the star as the focal point of either image; it ranked sixth in the list of what makes the object specific, behind the planets, the belt texture and the storage trays. Someone opening the box expecting the star to be the thing that stops them will instead find that the sixteen planets are the product and the star is a corner of the board. Everything else over-delivers; the one thing the design was built around under-delivers. The colour part of this is a known open item in the toolchain, not a geometry fault: the shop's colour contract takes raw sRGB channels and the preview renderer lights them linearly, so every named colour previews lighter than the filament will print.
resolution: Four rounds, the cap, and the last returns no blocking visual defect. It survives the hardest test available: a reader told nothing named all eight planets, read two armies of eight, read the grid as the grammar, read the sun and anti-sun as one geometry inverted at opposite poles of the board, read that the belt is terrain and that arriving at the opposing star is the win, and reconstructed the corona-as-trap mapping without ever seeing the word corona. Every candidate defect resolved against measurement: the flame feet stand wholly on the flange on one solid, the flange occupies exactly its own cell, the closest two pieces are 2.00 mm apart in all three states, the belt pad and every crest a disc can touch lie in one plane with nothing above it, and the black plug's missing relief is flat lambert on pure black rather than absent geometry. Two repairs came out of the rounds: a clip that sliced the flames was removed, and two markings that sat on the hidden hemisphere in every view were carried round their own axes to face the camera. Disclosed in full: after this review closed, `inspect validate` measured 22 assembly failures — ten self-intersecting colour bodies and twelve belt tiles with invalid topology — both were repaired in the geometry, and the 180-occurrence assembly now validates clean. The images were regenerated from the repaired sources and rebound here; the repair moved 0.84 per cent of the isometric's pixels and 1.17 per cent of the sheet's by more than eight levels, mean absolute change 0.24 and 0.27 of 255, so every blind observation above still describes the images it is bound to. No fifth round was taken; the budget was spent. Three Wish claims are recorded as not carrying at frame scale rather than as met: the obliquity lean as a silhouette cue, the rank numeral, and the disc taper.
reviewer: One independent native critic, four rounds. Each round: the two images alone with no brief, answers written and sealed, and only then the Wish and concept revealed.
